tier_reason: Peer-reviewed KDD 2024 paper (README BibTeX gives Proc. 30th ACM SIGKDD, pp. 2328-2339; DOI 10.1145/3637528.3671667 confirmed in search results) whose abstract claims up to 7.6x over partial-FT methods and optimized FFT libraries (FFTW, MKL); the repo README has no result table, no build files, no hardware and no flags, so not A.

corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed (KDD 2024) but the README has no result table, hardware or compiler flags, and the 7.6x figure is a maximum over all datasets and baselines (the abstract groups partial-FT methods and optimized FFT libraries together, so the max ratio may not be against FFTW or MKL). The paper PDF (author site, ACM DL, OpenReview) could not be opened from this container, so per-baseline numbers were not read. The baseline file src/FFTW.cpp includes the Windows-only tchar.h, the repo ships no Makefile or CMake file, and the code depends on Intel MKL and Intel IPP (proprietary, free-to-use) for the core routines. Computes only a subset of 2-D Fourier coefficients, not a full FFT. The predecessor PFT (snudatalab/PFT, KDD 2021, C++, Apache-2.0, 16 stars) makes the same kind of claim against FFTW and MKL but its README states no numbers.

notes: Repo, Apache-2.0 license, 3 stars and last commit 2025-08-19 (README edit) confirmed on github.com; stale is right (13 months). src/ holds Auto-MPFT.cpp (MKL DFTI + IPP), FFTW.cpp, PFT.cpp, Pruned FFT.cpp and Newton.cpp, but no build files. Paper unreachable (openreview.net, dl.acm.org, yongchanpark.github.io all blocked by egress).

tier_reason: ICLR 2024 paper (confirmed by search results pointing to the OpenReview forum and proceedings.iclr.cc PDF) plus README table on one H100-SXM against PyTorch FFT convolution; benchmark code (benchmarks/benchmark_flashfftconv.py) and nvcc flags (csrc/flashfftconv/setup.py) are public, but long-sequence rows are scaled from smaller batch/hidden sizes and the baseline runs in fp32 while FlashFFTConv runs fp16/bf16, so kept at B rather than A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table (gated convolution, one H100-SXM, all results scaled to batch 64, hidden 768; time units not stated in the table): 5.64x at 256, 7.93x at 1K, 6.64x at 4K, 5.42x at 8K, 2.45x at 16K, 3.22x at 32K, 1.74x at 1M, 1.37x at 2M, 1.30x at 4M (e.g. 1K: 0.29 vs 2.30); memory savings 2.81x-6.65x in the table; README text says 'up to 7.93 times faster than PyTorch FFT convolutions, with up to 8.21 times less memory usage' (the 8.21x memory figure is not in the table). The ICLR paper abstract (per search snippet) says up to 8.7x over PyTorch.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Nvidia PyTorch container 23.05, PyTorch 2.0, CUDA 12.1 toolkit; CUDA extension built with nvcc -O3 -lineinfo --use_fast_math -std=c++17 --generate-code=arch=compute_80,code=compute_80 and cxx -O3 (csrc/flashfftconv/setup.py)
corrections.caveats: The baseline is PyTorch's FFT convolution (torch.fft, cuFFT), not FFTW, MKL or KissFFT, and is a GPU task, so it only speaks to the cuFFT/PyTorch route. In benchmarks/benchmark_flashfftconv.py the PyTorch reference upcasts inputs to fp32 before torch.fft while FlashFFTConv runs in fp16 (bf16 also supported), so precision is not like-for-like. For sequence lengths of 16K and above the script shrinks batch and hidden size (set_B_H) and the README says results are scaled to batch 64, hidden 768. Gain shrinks to 1.3x at 4M tokens. The 8.21x memory claim in the README text exceeds the 6.65x maximum in its own table. The CUDA extension is compiled for compute_80 PTX only. Last commit December 2024.

notes: Repo, Apache-2.0, 355 stars, 37 forks, 35 commits, last commit 2024-12-28 confirmed on github.com; stale is right. Paper pages (arxiv.org, openreview.net) blocked by egress; venue taken from search results. GPU-only entry; consider whether the fft category should carry GPU-vs-PyTorch claims.

tier_reason: First-party sample self-test output in the README (7.11652x, 11523.3 vs 1619.23 ffts/sec); the test code (gpu_fftw_main.cpp show_speed) and Makefile flags are public, but the Pi model/CPU is not stated and the baseline FFTW plan uses FFTW_ESTIMATE, so C.

corrections.workload: Binary-compatible FFTW3 replacement that offloads power-of-two complex float FFTs (log2 N from 8 to 21) to the Raspberry Pi VideoCore GPU via Andrew Holme's GPU_FFT; the README self-test (gpu_fftw -t, show_speed in gpu_fftw_main.cpp) times 1000 forward 1024-point complex float FFTs against CPU fftw3f with an FFTW_ESTIMATE plan, excluding plan creation.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Makefile: gcc/g++ (or armv6l cross gcc) with -march=armv6 -mfloat-abi=hard -mfpu=vfp -mtune=arm1176jzf-s -O3 -ffast-math -pipe -fstack-protector (-std=c99 / -std=c++11); the README sample run does not state the compiler version or FFTW build used
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from one sample self-test output; Pi model and CPU clock not stated in the README (Makefile tunes for arm1176jzf-s, i.e. original BCM2835 Pi class). The FFTW baseline is planned with FFTW_ESTIMATE rather than FFTW_MEASURE, which handicaps FFTW, and only N=1024 is timed. Float precision only (optional 'double squashing' silently computes double requests in float); no 2-D, 3-D or real FFTs. Security: needs sudo/root to reach the GPU mailbox, and the README's 'Drop root permissions asap' TODO is unchecked; README calls it an early alpha. Bundled GPU_FFT (hello_fft/) is Andrew Holme's code under BSD-3-Clause, compatible with the project's MIT license. Repo is abandoned since January 2015.

notes: MIT license (LICENSE file, copyright placeholder 'John Doe'), 46 stars, 7 forks, 44 commits, last commit 2015-01-29 confirmed on github.com. Numbers match README exactly; 'up to ten times faster' is the README's description of GPU_FFT generally.
